data.sourceTitle: Early Migrations: Romans, Anglo-Saxons, and Vikings
data.targetTitle: Early Migrations: Romans, Anglo-Saxons, and Vikings
data.sourcePassage:
Britain has never been isolated from the rest of the world. Long before modern travel, the seas around Britain served as routes connecting it to Europe, Scandinavia, and the wider world. The first major wave of recorded migration came with the Roman conquest in 43 CE. Roman Britain was part of a vast empire stretching from North Africa to the Middle East, and soldiers, merchants, craftspeople, and enslaved people arrived from many different provinces. A Roman soldier stationed at Hadrian's Wall might come from modern Germany, Spain, or Syria. These migrants helped build towns such as Londinium, constructed roads, and introduced new foods, religions, and ideas.

After Roman authority weakened in the early fifth century, peoples known as the Angles, Saxons, and Jutes migrated from areas around modern Denmark and Germany to settle in Britain. Their migration was gradual and happened over many generations. It shaped the English language, giving us Old English, and left traces in thousands of place names ending in -ham, -ton, and -ing. From the late eighth century, Viking raids began, followed by settlement. Scandinavian people established themselves especially in northern and eastern England in an area known as the Danelaw. The Viking settlement also influenced place names — endings like -by and -thorpe — as well as law, trade, and culture.

In 1066 William, Duke of Normandy, conquered England. Though fewer in number than earlier migrations, the Normans wielded enormous power because they took control of land, law, and government. Norman French words entered the English language, the Domesday Book recorded landholdings, and castles appeared across the country. Each of these migrations changed Britain in lasting ways, from its language to its landscape, and challenged the idea that Britain was ever a single, unchanging people.

questions.question: In what year did the Roman conquest of Britain begin?
options: 43 CE
410 CE
793 CE
questions.modelAnswer: The Roman conquest of Britain began in 43 CE.

questions.question: What is the name for the area of northern and eastern England where Viking settlement was strongest?
options: Danelaw
Domesday
Normandy
Londinium
questions.modelAnswer: The area was called the Danelaw, where Danish Viking influence and law was strongest.

questions.question: Why did the Norman Conquest of 1066 have a powerful impact despite involving fewer migrants than earlier waves?
options: Because Normans were the first people to arrive in Britain
Because the Normans took control of land, law, and government, wielding enormous power
Because Norman migration was more peaceful than Viking raids
Because the Normans brought new farming techniques
questions.modelAnswer: The Norman Conquest had a powerful impact because the Normans took control of land, law, and government, giving them enormous power over English society despite being fewer in number.

questions.question: What does the fact that Roman soldiers came from Germany, Spain, and Syria suggest about Roman Britain?
options: Roman Britain was ruled entirely by Italians
Roman Britain was isolated from the rest of the empire
Roman Britain was part of a diverse, multinational empire with people from many provinces
Roman soldiers chose where to serve based on personal preference only
questions.modelAnswer: This shows that Roman Britain was part of a diverse, multinational empire. Soldiers were recruited from many different provinces across Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East, making Roman Britain a multicultural society connected to a vast imperial world.

data.sourcePassage:
Jewish communities settled in England after the Norman Conquest of 1066. Many lived in towns such as London, York, Lincoln, and Norwich. They contributed to trade, finance, and urban life, but they also faced severe restrictions. Medieval Christian law often barred Jewish people from many occupations, so some became involved in moneylending — one of the few roles available to them. Despite their economic contributions, Jewish communities were subjected to heavy taxation, false accusations, and violence. In 1190, many Jewish people in York were killed during a wave of anti-Jewish violence. In 1290, King Edward I ordered the expulsion of Jewish people from England. They were not officially permitted to resettle permanently until the seventeenth century.

Huguenots were French Protestants who fled France after Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685, removing legal protections for Protestants. Thousands came to England, settling in London, Canterbury, Norwich, and Bristol. They brought valuable skills in silk weaving, clockmaking, banking, and medicine. Over time, many Huguenot families integrated into British society, though they initially faced some suspicion and competition from local workers. Their influence can still be traced in certain family names and in the history of industries such as silk weaving in Spitalfields.

In the nineteenth century, Irish migration increased dramatically. The Great Famine of the 1840s, caused by potato blight and worsened by government failures, killed over a million people and drove millions more to emigrate. Many Irish migrants settled in Liverpool, Manchester, Glasgow, and London, working in construction, docks, and factories. They often faced anti-Irish and anti-Catholic prejudice, including poor housing, low-paid work, and social hostility. Despite this, Irish communities built churches, schools, newspapers, and strong political organisations, making lasting contributions to British working-class life.

questions.question: Why did Huguenots flee France after 1685?

Because Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes, removing legal protections for Protestants
Because there was a famine in France
Because they wanted to trade in English markets

questions.question: Why were some Jewish people in medieval England involved in moneylending?
options: Because it was the most profitable job available to anyone
Because medieval Christian law barred Jewish people from many other occupations
Because they brought the practice from other countries
Because the king ordered Jewish people to lend money
questions.modelAnswer: Jewish people became involved in moneylending partly because medieval Christian law barred them from many other occupations, making it one of the few economic roles available to them.

questions.question: What does the experience of both Jewish and Irish migrants suggest about the pattern of migration to Britain?
options: Migrants were always welcomed because Britain needed their skills
Migrants faced discrimination but still made significant contributions to British society
Migrants only came to Britain when invited by the government
British society was never hostile to newcomers
questions.modelAnswer: Both Jewish and Irish migrants faced serious discrimination — Jewish communities faced expulsion, violence, and false accusations, while Irish migrants faced anti-Irish and anti-Catholic prejudice. Yet both groups also made important contributions: Jewish communities contributed to trade and urban life, while Irish migrants built railways, churches, and communities. This shows that migration history involves both contribution and difficulty.

data.sourceTitle: The Windrush Generation and Post-War Migration
data.targetTitle: The Windrush Generation and Post-War Migration
data.sourcePassage:
A common myth is that African, Asian, and Caribbean people first arrived in Britain after the Second World War. In fact, people from these regions had lived in Britain for centuries — as sailors, soldiers, servants, writers, musicians, and campaigners. During the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, figures such as Olaudah Equiano and Ignatius Sancho showed that Black Britons were active in public and political life long before 1948.

However, 1948 became a powerful symbol when HMT Empire Windrush arrived at Tilbury in Essex on 22 June, carrying passengers from the Caribbean and elsewhere. Britain needed workers to help rebuild after the war and support the new National Health Service. People from the Caribbean, South Asia, Africa, and other Commonwealth countries had legal rights to come to Britain as British subjects. Windrush migrants worked in the NHS, on buses and trains, in factories, and in postal services. They built churches, newspapers, businesses, and vibrant community organisations.

Despite these contributions, many Windrush migrants also faced serious discrimination. Some landlords refused to house Black tenants. Some employers rejected applicants because of race. Racist violence occurred in some areas. South Asian migrants who came later in the 1950s and 1960s also faced prejudice in employment and public life. In 1972, Ugandan Asians expelled by Idi Amin were admitted to Britain, where many rebuilt successful lives. Migration from the Commonwealth transformed British food, music, sport, religion, and culture. Historians remind us that this story includes both remarkable achievement and painful injustice — and that a balanced view must acknowledge both.

questions.question: Why does the passage say a historian must acknowledge both 'remarkable achievement and painful injustice' when studying post-war migration?
options: Because post-war migration only involved achievement with no difficulties
Because treating migrants only as victims ignores their contributions, while focusing only on success ignores the racism and discrimination they faced
Because historians must always present two equal sides to every argument
Because the government decided migration was both good and bad at the same time
questions.modelAnswer: A balanced view is needed because both sides of the story are real and important. Treating migrants only as victims fails to recognise their huge contributions to British society, culture, and institutions. But focusing only on success ignores the very real discrimination, racism, and injustice that many migrants experienced in housing, employment, and public life. A complete historical account must include both.
